extracted.intended_audience: academics, researchers and graduate students in journalism/media studies and linguistics (also useful for media analysts and advanced journalism practitioners)
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing news values in news discourse
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and literature review for identifying, categorising and analysing 'news values' (selection criteria) across texts and images in news media; includes lists of specific news-value factors from multiple authors and guidance on how language, images and other semiotic resources construct newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brighton & Foy's 'new news values' (Relevance, Topicality, Composition, Expectation, Unusualness, Worth, External Factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brighton & Foy (2007) propose an updated set of 'new news values' — Relevance, Topicality, Composition, Expectation, Unusualness, Worth and External Factors — conceived as selection criteria ('a set of rules') applied to prioritise items, responsive to a 'cultural shift' between providers and consumers and suited to converged/digital media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They treat news values as 'pure' criteria external to mediated stories and include 'External influences' (e.g. proprietor, advertiser, politician) as a factor. They argue live television/news (e.g. 9/11) can exemplify unmediated or 'pure' news, illustrating how some events require no mediation to be prioritised. Use these values when analysing selection/priority decisions and to account for external pressures on selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill — 'picture opportunities' (visualisation as a news value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harcup & O'Neill identify a sub-category of the news value 'entertainment' labelled 'picture opportunities' and note that 'if a story provided a good picture opportunity then it was often included even when there was little obvious intrinsic newsworthiness'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They observe combinations such as a good picture combined with A-list celebrity, royalty, sex, TV, or a cuddly animal make items almost impossible for editors to resist. Use this criterion when assessing how availability of images drives selection, and when evaluating coverage that appears to prioritise visual appeal over other newsworthiness criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall's 'formal news value of the photographic sign'
rubrics_metrics.description: Hall (1973) describes a formal news value for press photographs: elaboration of photograph and text in terms of the professional ideology of news; photographic values include the unexpected, dramatic, recent event concerning a person of high status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between the 'formal' (surface/photographic features: unexpectedness, drama, recency, elite person) and the 'ideological' (connoted themes/interpretations). Use both levels when analysing photo selection and meaning-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craig's press-photograph news values (reference to elite persons, composition, personalization, negativity, conflict/dramatization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Craig (1994) identifies five news values at work in press photographs: reference to elite persons, composition, personalization, negativity, and conflict/dramatization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are photo-specific selection/interpretive values: assess how images reference elites, how composition choices focus or personalise subjects, and how negativity/conflict/dramatization are foregrounded to confer newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rössler et al.'s 'image-inherent news factors' (damage, violence/aggression, controversy, celebrities, unexpectedness, emotions, execution and technique, sexuality/eroticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rössler et al. (2011) catalogue photo news factors defined as 'selection criteria' that determine whether images are 'worth publishing', including damage, violence/aggression, controversy, celebrities, unexpectedness, emotions, execution/technique, and sexuality/eroticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these image-inherent factors when analysing photographic selection decisions or predicting publishability of images. They operate as explicit, image-focused heuristics for editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singletary & Lamb's yardstick for award-winning press photography (timeliness, proximity, conflict; proximity and human interest for feature photos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Singletary & Lamb (1984) measure news value in award-winning press photography using traditional values: for news photos the focus was timeliness, proximity and conflict; for feature photos the focus was proximity and human interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when distinguishing evaluative standards for news vs feature photography; emphasises timeliness/proximity/conflict as central in news-photo evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bell's taxonomy of news values (three groups and specific values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell (1991) categorises news values into three groups: (1) values relating to news content (Recency, Unexpectedness, Superlativeness), (2) values concerning news gathering/processing (Continuity, Competition, Prefabrication), and (3) values concerning the quality/style of the news text (Clarity, Brevity, Colour). He also treats some of these as 'goals' or 'aims' of news writing and editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Bell's taxonomy to analyse both why items are selected (content/gathering factors) and how texts are produced (stylistic goals). Bell emphasises that journalists can 'enhance' news value through language and editing—so evaluate both selection and linguistic/formal enhancement practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cotter's practice-based view (news values as internalised journalistic criteria: Timeliness, Proximity, Prominence etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cotter (2010) conceptualises news values as journalists' 'internalized assumptions about what is important to transmit' that function as guidelines/parameters creating a 'hierarchy of importance' used to decide what is news. She points to classic in-group taxonomies (Timeliness, Proximity, Prominence) and documents how news values are invoked explicitly in newsroom talk (e.g. 'It'll be a little old' for Recency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Cotter's perspective when analysing newsroom practice, talk and decision-making. Identify instances where news values are cited or invoked in meetings, memos or editorial justifications, and note how values affect placement, lede choice, sources, and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Van Dijk's cognitive constraints and news values (Novelty, Recency, Presupposition, Consonance, Relevance, Deviance/Negativity, Proximity plus production/economic constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Van Dijk (1988) differentiates news values arising from economic conditions, newsgathering production processes, and 'more specific cognitive constraints' including Novelty, Recency, Presupposition, Consonance, Relevance, Deviance and Negativity, and Proximity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this multi-level cognitive framing to account for both structural production constraints (budgets, deadlines, access) and the cognitive categories that make events interpretable as potential news. Analyses should consider circular influence between events and news discourse (events/texts mutually influence each other).

rubrics_metrics.name: News values as selection criteria driven by visualization/availability of images
rubrics_metrics.description: Across several studies the availability of images or 'visualization' is listed explicitly as a selection criterion: a good picture or picture opportunity can cause a story to be included even when intrinsic newsworthiness is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating editorial selection, treat image availability as an independent driver; examine how newsrooms prioritise stories because they afford strong visuals, and how this skews coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discursive approach: news values as discursively constructed (language, image, layout, typography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bednarek & Caple propose a 'discursive' approach where news values are seen as discursively constructed and 'newsworthiness becomes a quality of texts'. They aim to systematically categorise semiotic devices (language, photos/footage, layout, typography) used to construct newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this approach to analyse how linguistic and multimodal resources contribute to, express, enhance or relate to particular news values (e.g. lexical choices like 'reveal' enhance Unexpectedness; typographic emphasis or photo cropping can foreground Prominence). Applicable to published stories and to input texts (press releases, interviews) and newsroom discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic devices as mechanisms to construct/enhance news values
rubrics_metrics.description: Various authors note that particular linguistic choices function to construct or enhance news values: e.g., verbs like reveal/revelation/disclose enhance Unexpectedness; evaluative language can make Eliteness explicit (e.g. 'top psychologist Dr X'); anaphoric expressions can create Personalization; anonymous sources can be rhetorically constructed as 'elite'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding or evaluating news texts, include specific linguistic devices (lexical choices, tense, anaphora, evaluative phrases) as markers or enactors of news values. Analyses should catalogue these devices systematically to link textual features to inferred newsworthiness.
